problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized 
 by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\,{t}^{2}-t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{2}]?$
solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\,{t}^{2}-t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+t,$ and $y={t}^{2}-t.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)j \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t+1)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4t+1+4{t}^{2}-4t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{2}[({t}^{2}+t)-({t}^{2}-t)] \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2\sqrt{2}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j\,$ for $0\le t\le 1?$
solution:
Since $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})j \\  & =i+2tj \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{4y+1}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}\right)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1,\,t+1⟩$ for $t\in [0,3]?$
solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,t-1,\,t+1⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2},$ $y=t-1,$ and $z=t+1.$ 

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)k \\  & =2t\,i+j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2({t}^{2})-(t-1)^{2}-(t+1)^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-({t}^{2}-2t+1)-({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}+2t-1-{t}^{2}-2t-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2(2{t}^{2}+1)}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\,{t}^{2}-1,\,{t}^{2}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2]?$
solution:
Since $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\,{t}^{2}-1,\,{t}^{2}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+1,$ $y={t}^{2}-1,$ and $z={t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})k \\  & =2t\,i+2t\,j+2t\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t\ge0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =({t}^{2}+1)+({t}^{2}-1)-{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\,+t\,k$ for $\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
solution:
Since $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\,+t\,k,$ then along the curve we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ and $z=t.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, if $f(x,y,z)=z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =t((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}) \\  & =t({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
